content.rendered:
This free fake virus scan runs a convincing full-system malware scan that finds threats which do not exist. Launch it fullscreen and a progress bar climbs, file paths flash past, a files-scanned counter races upward, and a red “threats detected” number keeps ticking up. When the scan finishes, the screen turns into a full-blown infection warning and fake security alerts start piling up on top of each other. It is a completely harmless fake virus scan prank that runs entirely in your web browser — nothing is really scanned, no files are touched, and pressing ESC ends the whole thing instantly.

What the fake virus scan prank does

The tool imitates the moment an antivirus program finds something bad. A shield sits at the top of the screen next to a scan title, a progress bar fills at the speed you choose, and underneath it a line of text rattles through file paths like C:\Windows\System32\ntdll.dll and C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\svhost.exe. Two large counters track the damage: files scanned, which climbs into the thousands, and threats detected, which turns red as the number rises. Every detection is added to a running list with a realistic malware name and the file it was supposedly found in, so the fake antivirus scan builds tension the same way a real one does — slowly, and then all at once.

Two warning styles: Windows Security or classic red alert

A warning screen is only believable if it matches the machine it appears on, so the fake virus scan ships with two skins:

  • Windows Security scan — the calm blue-and-white look of a Microsoft Defender full scan, with the wording a real Windows machine uses (“Virus & threat protection”, “Full scan in progress. Do not turn off your computer.”). This is the more believable option on a Windows PC and works beautifully as a slow burn.
  • Classic red virus alert — the loud, old-school scareware screen: a dark background bathed in red, a pulsing border, a shaking warning shield and a blunt “Your computer is infected!” headline. It lands instantly and works on any operating system, which makes it the right pick for a Mac, a Chromebook or a phone.

Both styles run the same fake scan underneath. The difference is tone: one whispers that something might be wrong, the other screams it.

How to run the fake virus scan

Setting up the fake malware warning takes about ten seconds:

  1. Pick a warning style. Windows Security scan for a PC, classic red virus alert for anything else — or for maximum drama.
  2. Choose a scan speed. Fast finishes in about 15 seconds, Normal in about 45, and Slow stretches the fake virus scan out over roughly two minutes.
  3. Decide on alerts and sound. Leave the security alert pop-ups on for the full scareware effect, and tick the alarm if you want beeping once threats are “found”.
  4. Go fullscreen. Click “Start Fake Virus Scan” and the scan fills the entire display, hiding the browser tabs and address bar that would otherwise give the prank away.
  5. Exit whenever you like. Press ESC, or move the mouse and use the exit button in the corner. Everything stops at once and the page returns to normal.

The fake threats the scan “detects”

Detection names are what sell a fake virus alert. Generic wording like “a virus was found” reads as a joke immediately, so this scan uses names in the exact format antivirus engines use — Trojan:Win32/Wacatac.B!ml, Ransom:Win32/Cryptolocker.A, Backdoor:Win32/Bladabindi, Worm:Win32/Gamarue.I, HackTool:Win32/Keygen and more. Each one is paired with a plausible file path, so the list on screen reads exactly like a real quarantine report.

Every single one of them is invented. The names and paths are picked at random from a list written into the page, and none of them refers to anything on the computer running the fake virus scan. A web page cannot read your disk, and this one never tries.

Fake security alert pop-ups that multiply

Once the scan reaches 100%, the screen flips into its infected state: the title turns red, a warning banner appears across the bottom, and fake “Security Alert” windows start spawning across the display. Each one names a threat, shows the file it was found in, and offers two buttons — Ignore and Remove threat.

Neither button does anything except make the problem worse. Clicking “Remove threat” spawns two more alerts, and closing one with the X spawns another. That is precisely how real scareware behaves, and it is what turns a static fake malware warning into something people actually react to — the harder they try to fix it, the faster the screen fills up. If you would rather keep things calm, untick the pop-ups before launching and the prank stays as a straight scan-and-warning screen.

Set it up and walk away: a worked example

The most convincing way to use a fake virus scan is to start it and leave. Say you want a housemate to sit down to an apparently infected laptop:

  1. Open this page on their computer while they are away, and choose the Windows Security scan style so it matches their PC.
  2. Set the speed to Slow. A two-minute scan is still running when they walk back in, which is far more convincing than a screen that was clearly finished an hour ago.
  3. Turn the alarm sound off if you want them to discover it themselves rather than be called over by beeping.
  4. Launch it fullscreen and leave. They find a scan in progress, watch the threat counter climb, and then the alerts start stacking up.
  5. Reveal it quickly. One press of ESC and the machine is obviously fine — which is the moment the joke actually lands.

Why use a browser-based fake antivirus scan?

Most “fake virus” results ask you to install an app, sit through ads, or download a file — which is an odd thing to do in the name of a joke about malware. This fake virus scan prank is a single web page. It loads instantly, costs nothing, installs nothing, and leaves no trace once the tab is closed. There is no sign-up and no software that could slow the computer down.

It also beats playing a video of a scan, because it is live: the counters really count, the paths really change, the pop-ups really respond to clicks, and the scan length is whatever you set. Nobody has to sit still and hope the timing works out. And because it is an ordinary web page, the same link works on Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS, Android and iPhone.

Is the fake virus scan safe?

Completely. The fake virus scan is an animation made of HTML, CSS and JavaScript running inside a browser tab. It does not read, open, move, encrypt or delete a single file. It installs nothing, changes no settings, and downloads nothing to the device. The file paths, threat names, file counts and timers are all generated on the page for show.

Because there are no executables and no downloads, antivirus and anti-malware software treats this page like any other website — there is nothing here for it to flag. When you press ESC, the scan, the alerts and the alarm all stop together and nothing keeps running in the background. The computer is in exactly the state it was in before you started.

Fake virus scan vs. a real antivirus scan

A real scan runs inside an application window with the usual system chrome around it, keeps a history you can open later, and lets you actually quarantine or remove what it finds. It also survives a restart: real detections are still there when you reboot. This fake virus alert does none of that. It lives in a browser tab, its buttons lead nowhere, and one press of ESC wipes it out permanently.

That is the reassurance to hand anyone who falls for it — if a warning disappears when you close a browser tab, it was never a real infection. It is also worth knowing in reverse: genuine malware warnings never arrive as a web page demanding you call a phone number or install a “cleaner”. If you want to check a machine properly, run Windows Security, Microsoft Defender, or whatever antivirus product you already trust.

Fake virus scan on a phone or Mac

The prank works in any modern mobile browser, so you can hand someone a phone that appears to be mid-scan and watch the threat counter climb. On Android, iPhone, or a Mac, choose the classic red virus alert style: a Windows Security screen on an iPhone reads as fake immediately, while a red infection warning looks plausible anywhere. The layout adapts to smaller screens, so the counters, the detection list and the alerts all stay readable on a phone.

Tips for a believable fake malware warning

  • Always go fullscreen. A visible address bar ruins the illusion faster than anything else on this list.
  • Match the style to the machine — Windows Security on a PC, red alert everywhere else.
  • Prefer Slow or Normal speed. A scan that finishes in 15 seconds looks like an animation; one that grinds along looks like work.
  • Let them click. The pop-ups multiplying under their own clicks is the funniest part of the fake virus scan — do not rush in to explain.
  • Keep the alarm for a crowd. Sound helps when other people are in the room, but it gives the game away faster one-on-one.

Prank responsibly

A convincing infection warning is stronger medicine than most screen pranks. Real scareware exists precisely because these screens work: people panic, call the number on the screen, hand over card details, or wipe a drive they did not need to wipe. Keep this one to friends, family and colleagues who will laugh, stay in the room, and reveal the trick quickly with ESC. Never use a fake virus scan on a stranger, on someone who is nervous about their computer, or as a way to sell anything or push someone into installing software — at that point it stops being a prank and becomes a scam.

More prank screens

If a scan is not quite the joke you are after, the fake Blue Screen of Death makes a PC look like it has crashed outright, the hacker typer turns any keyboard into a wall of scrolling code, and the cracked screen prank makes the display itself look shattered. The full set lives on the prank screens page — all of them browser-based, all of them undone by a single press of ESC.

That is the whole trick: pick a style, pick a speed, go fullscreen, and let the fake virus scan do the rest. The threats are invented, the alerts lead nowhere, and the computer was never in any danger at all.
